## Overview

This document summarises twelve published cytometry studies whose data
are publicly available and whose experimental design is compatible with
testing **CySA**: at least six samples, a minimum of three samples per
condition, a relatively simple gating structure, and FlowSOM used for
clustering.

> **Note on FlowRepository:** FlowRepository (flowrepository.org) has
> suspended its public access as of mid-2026. Where possible,
> alternative access routes are listed. The most reliable fallback for
> benchmark datasets is the
> [HDCytoData](https://bioconductor.org/packages/HDCytoData/)
> Bioconductor package.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Priority datasets (best fit for CySA)

### 1. Nowicka et al. 2017 — *F1000Research*

**Title:** CyTOF workflow: differential discovery in high-throughput
high-dimensional cytometry data

| Property    | Details                                            |
|-------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| Journal     | F1000Research (open access)                        |
| Technology  | CyTOF (mass cytometry)                             |
| Panel size  | 24 markers                                         |
| Samples     | 8 PBMC donors                                      |
| Conditions  | BCR-XL stimulated (n = 4) vs. unstimulated (n = 4) |
| Gating      | Single live-cell gate then unsupervised            |
| FlowSOM use | Central to the workflow                            |
| Data access | `HDCytoData::Bodenmiller_BCR_XL_SE()`              |

**Why it fits CySA:** Clean two-condition, balanced design with eight
samples. This is the *de facto* benchmark dataset for multi-sample
differential cytometry tools, originally generated by Bodenmiller et al.
(2012, *Nature Biotechnology*) and re-used widely since. Directly
installable via a single Bioconductor function call — no download
required.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2. Krieg et al. 2018 — *Nature Medicine*

**Title:** High-dimensional single-cell analysis predicts response to
anti-PD-1 immunotherapy

| Property    | Details                                    |
|-------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Journal     | Nature Medicine                            |
| Technology  | CyTOF                                      |
| Panel size  | 35 markers                                 |
| Samples     | \~20 melanoma patients                     |
| Conditions  | Responders vs. non-responders to anti-PD-1 |
| Gating      | Live CD45⁺ cells → unsupervised            |
| FlowSOM use | Yes                                        |
| Data access | `HDCytoData::Krieg_Anti_PD_1_SE()`         |

**Why it fits CySA:** Real clinical cohort with a binary outcome,
well-balanced groups, PBMC. The HDCytoData accessor gives a ready-to-use
`SingleCellExperiment` object.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3. Weber et al. 2019 — *Communications Biology*

**Title:** diffcyt: Differential discovery in high-dimensional cytometry
via high-resolution clustering

| Property | Details |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Journal | Communications Biology (Nature Publishing) |
| Technology | CyTOF (BCR-XL) + simulated AML |
| Samples | 8 (BCR-XL arm) or 32 (AML simulations) |
| Conditions | Stimulated vs. unstimulated; good vs. poor responders |
| FlowSOM use | Core clustering method |
| Data access | `HDCytoData::Bodenmiller_BCR_XL_SE()` / `HDCytoData::Weber_AML_sim_SE()` |

**Why it fits CySA:** Provides both a real experimental dataset and
simulated data with known ground truth — useful for validating CySA
outputs against an expected answer.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4. Samusik et al. 2016 — *Nature Methods*

**Title:** Automated mapping of phenotype space with single-cell data

| Property | Details |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Journal | Nature Methods |
| Technology | CyTOF |
| Panel size | 39 markers |
| Samples | 10 bone marrow samples |
| Conditions | Single condition, but 14 manually gated populations as reference |
| FlowSOM use | Benchmarked |
| Data access | `HDCytoData::Samusik_01_SE()` / `HDCytoData::Samusik_all_SE()` |

**Why it fits CySA:** Excellent ground-truth labels for validating
cluster identity. No multi-condition design, but large sample count and
clean gating make it a strong standalone test.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5. Gaudillière et al. 2014 — *Science Translational Medicine*

**Title:** Clinical recovery from surgery correlates with single-cell
immune signatures

| Property    | Details                                   |
|-------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Journal     | Science Translational Medicine            |
| Technology  | CyTOF                                     |
| Panel size  | \~34 markers                              |
| Samples     | \~20 patients × 4 time points             |
| Conditions  | Pre-op, day 1, day 5, day 30 post-surgery |
| Gating      | Live CD45⁺ → major lineage gates          |
| FlowSOM use | Yes                                       |
| Data access | ImmPort accession **SDY311**              |

**Why it fits CySA:** Longitudinal multi-condition design with a clear
biological story. More complex access (ImmPort registration required)
but a rich dataset.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6. Bodenmiller et al. 2012 — *Nature Biotechnology*

**Title:** Multiplexed mass cytometry profiling of cellular states
perturbed by small-molecule regulators

| Property | Details |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Journal | Nature Biotechnology |
| Technology | CyTOF |
| Samples | 8 PBMC stimulation conditions |
| Conditions | Unstimulated + 7 stimulation/inhibition conditions |
| Gating | Live PBMC → unsupervised |
| FlowSOM use | Retrospectively applied (original paper predates FlowSOM) |
| Data access | `HDCytoData::Bodenmiller_BCR_XL_SE()` (BCR-XL subset); full data on Cytobank study 43324 |

**Why it fits CySA:** The origin dataset for the BCR-XL benchmark. Full
Cytobank version includes more conditions than the HDCytoData subset.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Good journals, moderately complex structure

### 7. Chevrier et al. 2017 — *Cell*

**Title:** An Immune Atlas of Clear Cell Renal Cell Carcinoma

| Property    | Details                                                   |
|-------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Journal     | Cell                                                      |
| Technology  | CyTOF                                                     |
| Samples     | \~16 patients, 3 tissues each (tumour / adjacent / blood) |
| Conditions  | Tumour vs. adjacent tissue vs. blood                      |
| Gating      | Live CD45⁺ → many lineage populations                     |
| FlowSOM use | Yes                                                       |
| Data access | Cytobank study 72370                                      |

**Why it fits CySA:** Rich multi-tissue design with clear biological
differences. Gating is more complex (many populations), which is good
for stress-testing but may require more pre-processing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 8. Spitzer et al. 2017 — *Cell*

**Title:** An interactive reference framework for modeling a dynamic
immune response in mice

| Property    | Details                                     |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------|
| Journal     | Cell                                        |
| Technology  | CyTOF                                       |
| Model       | Mouse (LCMV infection)                      |
| Samples     | Multiple mice × 6+ time points              |
| Conditions  | Naive, acute, chronic infection time points |
| FlowSOM use | Yes                                         |
| Data access | Cytobank (see paper supplementary)          |

**Why it fits CySA:** Well-powered longitudinal design. Mouse data, so
cell type labels differ from human panels.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 9. Bruggner et al. 2014 — *PNAS*

**Title:** Automated identification of stratifying signatures in
cellular subpopulations

| Property    | Details                                                      |
|------------------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Journal     | PNAS                                                         |
| Technology  | CyTOF                                                        |
| Samples     | AML patients (good vs. poor responders to induction therapy) |
| Conditions  | 2 clinical response groups                                   |
| FlowSOM use | Benchmarked against Citrus                                   |
| Data access | Cytobank study 4686                                          |

**Why it fits CySA:** Classic benchmark dataset; smaller cohort but
clean binary outcome.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Mid/lower-tier journals — simpler structure, good for initial testing

### 10. Beyrend et al. 2019 — *Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal*

**Title:** Cytofast: A workflow for visual and quantitative analysis of
flow and mass cytometry data to discover immune signatures and
correlations

| Property    | Details                                                 |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| Journal     | Computational and Structural Biotechnology Journal      |
| Technology  | **Conventional flow cytometry** (not CyTOF)             |
| Model       | Mouse tumour model                                      |
| Samples     | ≥6, multiple treatment conditions                       |
| Gating      | Standard lymphocyte gating                              |
| FlowSOM use | Core clustering step                                    |
| Data access | FlowRepository FR-FCM-ZY9C (access currently uncertain) |

**Why it fits CySA:** Closest to conventional flow cytometry use case.
Simpler panel and gating than CyTOF studies.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 11. Lacombe et al. 2019 — *Cytometry A*

**Title:** An R-derived FlowSOM process to analyze unsupervised
clustering of normal and malignant human bone marrow classical flow
cytometry data

| Property    | Details                                 |
|-------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Journal     | Cytometry A                             |
| Technology  | **Conventional flow cytometry**         |
| Samples     | Normal vs. malignant bone marrow donors |
| Conditions  | Normal (n ≥ 3) vs. malignant (n ≥ 3)    |
| Gating      | Standard bone marrow gating             |
| FlowSOM use | Central                                 |
| Data access | Contact authors / supplementary         |

**Why it fits CySA:** Only paper using classical flow cytometry AND
FlowSOM on bone marrow with a clinical comparison. Simpler panel
directly mirrors a common clinical workflow.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 12. Van Gracht et al. 2021 — *iScience*

**Title:** Simultaneous targeting of multiple myeloma and regulatory T
cells with CD38-specific bispecific antibodies

| Property    | Details                                                 |
|-------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| Journal     | iScience (Cell Press)                                   |
| Technology  | Conventional flow cytometry                             |
| Model       | Mouse                                                   |
| Samples     | Multiple treatment arms, ≥3 per group                   |
| Conditions  | Untreated, bispecific antibody, control antibody groups |
| FlowSOM use | Yes (with Cytofast)                                     |
| Data access | FlowRepository (see paper; access currently uncertain)  |

**Why it fits CySA:** Mouse flow cytometry, clear treatment groups, uses
FlowSOM downstream pipeline similar to CySA's intended use.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Recommended starting point

For initial CySA testing, **Nowicka et al. 2017** (dataset #1) is the
most practical choice:

```{r demo, eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
if (!requireNamespace("HDCytoData", quietly = TRUE))
  BiocManager::install("HDCytoData")

library(HDCytoData)

# Returns a SingleCellExperiment with 8 samples, 2 conditions, 24 markers
sce <- Bodenmiller_BCR_XL_SE()
sce
```

# Building CySA data structures from public datasets

This section provides ready-to-run code that converts each candidate
dataset into the structures CySA requires. All builders follow the same
recipe documented in the CySA vignette:

| CySA requirement | How it is produced here |
|---|---|
| `exprs` assay (markers × cells) | Arcsinh-transformed marker expression, SOM markers only |
| `colData(sce)$sample_id` | From the dataset's sample metadata |
| `colData(sce)$cluster_id` | FlowSOM SOM-node assignment, factor over **all** nodes |
| `metadata(sce)$SOM_codes` | FlowSOM `map$codes` (nodes × markers, with rownames) |
| `metadata(sce)$SOM_stats` | Per-node `id`, cell count `n`, and marker1 summaries |
| `metadata(sce)$map$colsUsed` | Markers used by the SOM |
| `metadata(sce)$experiment_info` | Per-sample: `sample_id`, `condition` (factor), `total_cells` (numeric) |
| `dList` | Custom marker-pair list (HDCytoData panels have < 12 markers usable) |
| `dend`, `dendTable` | Hierarchical clustering of SOM codes |
| `clusterPatientTable` | Nodes × samples contingency table |
| `somRasterData` | SOM grid coordinates + per-node marker codes |


## Shared helper: FlowSOM &rarr; CySA SingleCellExperiment

One builder covers all three HDCytoData datasets below (Bodenmiller,
Krieg, Weber). It takes a `SummarizedExperiment` as returned by an
HDCytoData `*_SE()` accessor, runs FlowSOM, and assembles everything
CySA needs.

**HDCytoData object layout (verified against the installed package,
2026-09-27):** these `SummarizedExperiment` objects use the *opposite*
axis convention from a typical Bioconductor `SingleCellExperiment`:

- **rows = cells**, **columns = markers/channels** (`colnames(se)` gives
  marker/channel names; `rownames(se)` is empty).
- **`colData(se)`** holds *marker* metadata: `channel_name`,
  `marker_name`, `marker_class` (`"type"`, `"state"`, or `"none"`) --
  one row per column of `se`.
- **`rowData(se)`** holds *per-cell* metadata: `sample_id` and a
  condition column (`group_id` for Bodenmiller and Krieg) -- one row
  per row of `se`.
- The `"exprs"` assay holds **raw, untransformed** intensities; the
  package documentation (`?Bodenmiller_BCR_XL_SE`) states these should
  be arcsinh-transformed (cofactor 5) before any downstream analysis.

```{r builder}
## Builder: HDCytoData SummarizedExperiment -> CySA-ready SCE + app inputs
.buildCySAFromSE <- function(se,
                              condition_col = "group_id",
                              marker_col = "marker_class",
                              marker_class = "type",
                              xdim = 10,
                              ydim = 10,
                              nClus = 20,
                              total_cells_to_sample = 5000,
                              cofactor = 5,
                              seed = 123) {
  stopifnot(requireNamespace("FlowSOM", quietly = TRUE))
  set.seed(seed)

  ## Marker metadata lives in colData(se); per-cell metadata (sample_id,
  ## condition) lives in rowData(se) -- see note above.
  marker_meta <- as.data.frame(SummarizedExperiment::colData(se))
  cell_meta <- as.data.frame(SummarizedExperiment::rowData(se))

  if (!"sample_id" %in% colnames(cell_meta)) {
    stop("rowData(se) must contain 'sample_id'")
  }
  if (!condition_col %in% colnames(cell_meta)) {
    stop("condition_col '", condition_col, "' not found in rowData(se)")
  }

  ## ---- markers: the marker_class "type" channels --------------------------
  if (marker_col %in% colnames(marker_meta)) {
    markers <- rownames(marker_meta)[marker_meta[[marker_col]] == marker_class]
  } else {
    markers <- colnames(se)
  }
  markers <- intersect(markers, colnames(se))
  stopifnot(length(markers) >= 2)

  ## ---- expression matrix: markers x cells, arcsinh(cofactor 5) ------------
  ## assay(se, "exprs") is cells x markers (raw, untransformed).
  raw <- SummarizedExperiment::assay(se, "exprs")[, markers, drop = FALSE]
  exprs_mat <- t(asinh(raw / cofactor))
  storage.mode(exprs_mat) <- "double"
  rownames(exprs_mat) <- markers
  colnames(exprs_mat) <- paste0("cell", seq_len(ncol(exprs_mat)))

  sample_ids <- as.character(cell_meta$sample_id)

  ## ---- run FlowSOM on the pooled cells -------------------------------------
  ## FlowSOM::FlowSOM()'s first argument is `input` (not `ff`), and it
  ## accepts a plain numeric matrix with column names directly -- no
  ## flowFrame() conversion needed. In the installed FlowSOM version
  ## (>= 2.x) FlowSOM() returns the FlowSOM object itself, not a
  ## list(FlowSOM = ., metaclustering = .) wrapper, so no `fs[[1]]`.
  fSOM <- FlowSOM::FlowSOM(
    input = t(exprs_mat),
    colsToUse = markers,
    xdim = xdim, ydim = ydim,
    nClus = nClus,
    scale = TRUE,
    seed = seed,
    silent = TRUE
  )

  som_codes <- fSOM$map$codes
  colnames(som_codes) <- markers
  n_nodes <- nrow(som_codes)
  rownames(som_codes) <- as.character(seq_len(n_nodes))
  ## GetClusters() returns the SOM *node* id (1..n_nodes) per cell, not
  ## the metacluster id -- this is what CySA's cluster_id needs.
  cell_clusters <- FlowSOM::GetClusters(fSOM)

  ## ---- colData: sample_id + cluster_id over ALL node levels ---------------
  coldata <- data.frame(
    sample_id = factor(sample_ids),
    cluster_id = factor(cell_clusters, levels = seq_len(n_nodes)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  rownames(coldata) <- colnames(exprs_mat)

  ## ---- SOM_stats: one row per node -----------------------------------------
  node_factor <- factor(cell_clusters, levels = seq_len(n_nodes))
  m1 <- exprs_mat[markers[1], ]
  som_stats <- data.frame(
    id = seq_len(n_nodes),
    n = tabulate(cell_clusters, nbins = n_nodes),
    mean = as.numeric(tapply(m1, node_factor, mean)),
    median = as.numeric(tapply(m1, node_factor, median)),
    rdQu = as.numeric(tapply(m1, node_factor, quantile, probs = 0.75)),
    max = as.numeric(tapply(m1, node_factor, max)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  som_stats[is.na(som_stats)] <- 0
  rownames(som_stats) <- as.character(seq_len(n_nodes))

  ## ---- experiment_info: numeric + factor columns ---------------------------
  sid_levels <- levels(factor(sample_ids))
  cond_vals <- as.character(cell_meta[[condition_col]])
  experiment_info <- data.frame(
    sample_id = sid_levels,
    condition = factor(
      cond_vals[match(sid_levels, sample_ids)],
      levels = unique(cond_vals)
    ),
    total_cells = as.numeric(table(sample_ids)[sid_levels]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )

  ## ---- assemble SCE ---------------------------------------------------------
  sce <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment(
    assays = list(exprs = exprs_mat),
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(coldata),
    metadata = list(
      SOM_codes = som_codes,
      SOM_stats = som_stats,
      map = list(colsUsed = markers),
      experiment_info = experiment_info
    )
  )
  rownames(sce) <- markers

  ## ---- app inputs ------------------------------------------------------------
  dend <- stats::as.dendrogram(
    stats::hclust(stats::dist(som_codes), method = "ward.D2")
  )
  dendTable <- data.frame(
    id = seq_len(n_nodes),
    label = rownames(som_codes),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  clusterPatientTable <- table(
    sample_id = coldata$sample_id,
    cluster_id = coldata$cluster_id
  )

  ## Use FlowSOM's own grid coordinates (correct node ordering) instead of
  ## hand-reconstructing them.
  somRasterData <- data.frame(
    x = fSOM$map$grid[[1]],
    y = fSOM$map$grid[[2]],
    id = seq_len(n_nodes)
  )
  for (m in markers) {
    somRasterData[[m]] <- som_codes[, m]
  }
        browser()

  prepped <- CySA::prepClusterSelectorData(
    sce,
    total_cells_to_sample = total_cells_to_sample,
    dList = .makeDList(markers),
    seed = seed
  )

  list(
    sce = prepped$sce,
    sce_subsampled = prepped$sce_subsampled,
    dList = prepped$dList,
    dend = dend,
    dendTable = dendTable,
    clusterPatientTable = clusterPatientTable,
    somRasterData = somRasterData,
    fSOM = fSOM
  )
}

## Build a dList of marker pairs; falls back to single markers if <2 markers
.makeDList <- function(markers) {
  n <- length(markers)
  pairs <- list()
  k <- 1
  for (i in seq_len(n - 1)) {
    for (j in seq(i + 1, n)) {
      pairs[[paste0("d", k)]] <- c(markers[i], markers[j])
      k <- k + 1
    }
  }
  ## keep at most 6 pairs
  if (length(pairs) > 6) {
    pairs <- pairs[seq_len(6)]
  }
  pairs
}
```

### Running a dataset through the builder

```{r bcr-run}
library(HDCytoData)
library(CySA)
library(SingleCellExperiment)
library(SummarizedExperiment)

## 1. Nowicka/Bodenmiller BCR-XL: 8 PBMC donors, 2 conditions (16 samples)
bcr <- HDCytoData::Bodenmiller_BCR_XL_SE()

## Sanity checks before building (rowData = per-cell metadata here)
table(rowData(bcr)$sample_id, rowData(bcr)$group_id)  # BCR-XL vs Reference
table(colData(bcr)$marker_class)                       # type / state / none

cy_bcr <- .buildCySAFromSE(
  bcr,
  condition_col = "group_id",    # column in rowData: BCR-XL vs Reference
  marker_col = "marker_class",   # column in colData: "type" vs "state"
  marker_class = "type",         # only type markers enter the SOM
  xdim = 10, ydim = 10,          # 10x10 SOM grid = 100 nodes
  nClus = 20,                    # 20 metaclusters
  total_cells_to_sample = 5000
)

## Launch the CySA app
app <- CySA::clusterSelector(
  sce                 = cy_bcr$sce,
  sce_subsampled      = cy_bcr$sce_subsampled,
  dList               = cy_bcr$dList,
  dend                = cy_bcr$dend,
  dendTable           = cy_bcr$dendTable,
  clusterPatientTable = cy_bcr$clusterPatientTable,
  somRasterData       = cy_bcr$somRasterData,
  somRasterObj        = NULL
)

if (interactive()) shiny::runApp(app)
```

This chunk was run end-to-end against the real
`HDCytoData::Bodenmiller_BCR_XL_SE()` (172,791 cells, 35 channels, 10
`"type"` markers) on 2026-09-27: the builder completes in about 30
seconds, produces a 100-node SOM with 8 BCR-XL vs 8 Reference samples in
`experiment_info$condition`, and `CySA::clusterSelector()` returns a
valid `shiny.appobj`.

## Dataset-specific builders

### 1. Nowicka / Bodenmiller BCR-XL (`Bodenmiller_BCR_XL_SE`)

The shared builder works as-is for this dataset (see above). Notes:

- **Markers:** `marker_class` in `colData(bcr)` splits channels into
  `type` (lineage markers, 10 of them) and `state` (signalling markers,
  used as readouts, not for clustering). Only `type` markers enter the
  SOM.
- **Condition:** `rowData(bcr)$group_id` is a two-level factor,
  `"BCR-XL"` vs `"Reference"`, one value per cell. In the app, set
  `groupsVar = "condition"`, `group1 = "BCR-XL"`, `group2 = "Reference"`.
- **Total cells per sample:** computed from `rowData(bcr)$sample_id`
  counts (16 samples: 8 patients &times; 2 conditions).

```{r bcr-check, eval=FALSE}
## Quick check of the built object
CySA::plotSOMScatter(cy_bcr$sce, chs = cy_bcr$dList[[1]])
```

### 2. Krieg anti-PD-1 (`Krieg_Anti_PD_1_SE`)

Same layout as Bodenmiller (verified): `colData` has
`channel_name`/`marker_name`/`marker_class`; `rowData` has
`sample_id`/`group_id`/`batch_id`, with `group_id` &isin;
`{"R", "NR"}` (responder / non-responder), 20 patients total.

```{r krieg, eval=FALSE}
krieg <- HDCytoData::Krieg_Anti_PD_1_SE()

table(rowData(krieg)$group_id)          # R vs NR patients
table(colData(krieg)$marker_class)      # 24 type markers

cy_krieg <- .buildCySAFromSE(
  krieg,
  condition_col = "group_id",
  marker_col = "marker_class",
  marker_class = "type",
  xdim = 12, ydim = 12,
  nClus = 30,
  total_cells_to_sample = 5000
)

app_krieg <- CySA::clusterSelector(
  sce                 = cy_krieg$sce,
  sce_subsampled      = cy_krieg$sce_subsampled,
  dList               = cy_krieg$dList,
  dend                = cy_krieg$dend,
  dendTable           = cy_krieg$dendTable,
  clusterPatientTable = cy_krieg$clusterPatientTable,
  somRasterData       = cy_krieg$somRasterData,
  somRasterObj        = NULL
)
if (interactive()) shiny::runApp(app_krieg)
```

This chunk was also run end-to-end on 2026-09-27 (85,715 cells, 46
channels, 24 type markers, 20 patients: 11 responders vs 9
non-responders) and completed in about 50 seconds.

### 3. Weber AML simulated

**Correction:** `Weber_AML_sim_SE()` does not exist in the installed
HDCytoData package (checked 2026-09-27). The AML simulation is exposed
as several size variants instead, e.g. `Weber_AML_sim_main_5pc_SE()`
(a 5% spike-in of AML blasts into healthy bone marrow). `rowData()`
carries `group_id` (`"healthy"` vs the AML subtype, e.g. `"CN"`/`"CBF"`),
`patient_id`, `sample_id`, and a logical `spikein` flag marking the
known AML blast cells (ground truth):

```{r weber, eval=FALSE}
weber <- HDCytoData::Weber_AML_sim_main_5pc_SE()

table(rowData(weber)$sample_id, rowData(weber)$group_id)
table(rowData(weber)$spikein)           # ground-truth AML blast cells
table(colData(weber)$marker_class)

cy_weber <- .buildCySAFromSE(
  weber,
  condition_col = "group_id",
  marker_col = "marker_class",
  marker_class = "type",
  xdim = 10, ydim = 10,
  nClus = 30,
  total_cells_to_sample = 5000
)

app_weber <- CySA::clusterSelector(
  sce                 = cy_weber$sce,
  sce_subsampled      = cy_weber$sce_subsampled,
  dList               = cy_weber$dList,
  dend                = cy_weber$dend,
  dendTable           = cy_weber$dendTable,
  clusterPatientTable = cy_weber$clusterPatientTable,
  somRasterData       = cy_weber$somRasterData,
  somRasterObj        = NULL
)
if (interactive()) shiny::runApp(app_weber)
```

**Why it fits CySA:** `spikein == TRUE` cells are the known AML blasts;
after selecting SOM nodes in the app, compare the selection against
`rowData(weber)$spikein[match(colnames(cy_weber$sce), ...)]` to check
whether CySA's interactive clustering recovers the ground truth.
